title: The Unix Philosophy — Do One Thing Well, Pipe It Together

panels.prompt: A distinguished older man in a 1970s collared shirt standing at a whiteboard, enthusiastically drawing a diagram of garden hoses screwed together end-to-end with water flowing through them, arrows showing data flow, other researchers watching with interest, bright fluorescent lab lighting, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, purple accent on the whiteboard drawings
panels.label: Doug McIlroy at the whiteboard — the garden hose analogy for Unix pipes

panels.text: Doug McIlroy, the head of the department where Unix was born, had been championing an idea since the early 1960s. In a 1964 memo, he wrote: "We should have some ways of coupling programs like garden hoses — screw in another segment when it becomes necessary to massage data in another way."

panels.text: In 1973, Thompson implemented it. The pipe — represented by the | symbol — allowed the output of one program to flow directly into the input of another. Before pipes, you had to save intermediate files at every stage. Pipes eliminated the friction and made composing small programs feel natural.

panels.text: McIlroy articulated the Unix philosophy: "Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface."

panels.text: Don't build a Swiss Army knife. Build a knife, a screwdriver, and a can opener — and make them work together. The power is in the composition, not in any single tool. Remember this idea. It will come back 55 years later, in a very surprising way.

Unix had a philosophy. It had pipes. But it was still written in assembly — still chained to one machine. To break that chain, Dennis Ritchie was building something: a new programming language named after a letter of the alphabet.
